Non-GAAP gross profit is the Company’s gross profit with adjustments to add back depreciation and amortization related to cost of revenue. Non-GAAP gross margin is defined as non-GAAP gross profit divided by revenue. Reconciliations of each of these non-GAAP financial measures to the most closely comparable GAAP financial measure, including a breakdown of the excluded items noted above are included following the financial statements attached to this news release. These non-GAAP financial measures are not calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP and should not be considered as an alternative to net income (loss), operating income (loss), gross profit, gross margin or any other financial measures so calculated and presented, nor as an alternative to cash flow from operating activities as a measure of liquidity. The Company has provided these non-GAAP financial measures and KPI because management believes such information to be important supplemental measures of performance that are commonly used by securities analysts, investors and other interested parties in the evaluation of companies in its industry. Management also uses this information internally for forecasting, budgeting and measuring annual bonus compensation targets for executive personnel, including the Company’s named executive officers. Non-GAAP net income (loss) provides management and investors consistency and comparability with the Company’s past financial performance and facilitates period-to-period comparisons of operations, as it eliminates the effect of items that are often unrelated to overall operating performance. Non-GAAP gross profit and non-GAAP gross margin allow investors and the Company’s management team to analyze the Company’s operating performance by excluding expenses that are not directly related to the cost of providing goods and services. title: 4 AI Workflows Built With Grain + Claude (And How to Copy Them)
summary: How three Grain founders use the new Claude connector to run AI workflows for meeting prep, daily engineering briefs, knowledge graphs, and Slack alignment.
body_text: How three Grain leaders use the new Claude connector to run meeting prep, daily engineering briefs, knowledge graphs, and Slack alignment workflows. With folder structures, exact prompts, and the verbatim quotes from each speaker. TL;DR Grain's new Claude connector lets Claude pull meeting transcripts, notes, action items, and clips on demand. No copy-pasting. Mike Adams (co-founder) runs an AI knowledge vault: three folders ( Raw , Wiki , Output ) plus a CLAUDE.md file. It generates sales decks, marketing assets, and product strategy from a knowledge graph built out of his meetings. Jeff Whitlock (CEO) replaced two of five weekly standups with a scheduled Claude task that posts an engineering daily brief to his Slack DMs. Ben DeMordaunt (Head of Ops) built a daily meeting prep skill live in about 10 minutes. It pulls Google Calendar, searches Grain for past recordings with the same attendees, and posts a brief to Slack every morning. Mike also demoed a trigger-based Slack alignment workflow that combines Grain MCP, Slack MCP, Amplitude MCP, and Figma in a single Claude prompt. Thomas Tabi (Customer Success Lead) closed the session with the most important reminder: "I'm not technical, but I get Claude to do whatever I want." You don't need an engineering background to build any of these. The pattern across all four: output lives in tools where work already happens (Slack, Linear, local files), meetings are the context layer, and every workflow started simple before it got powerful. Why most AI rollouts stall Most AI rollouts impress in the demo and then quietly disappear from your weekly routine. The problem usually isn't the tool. It's that nobody wired it into the work that actually happens every day. Last week, three of us at Grain spent 30 minutes walking through the AI workflows we use every week. Not demos. Not hypotheticals. The ones running right now. Mike showed how he built a personal knowledge graph from his meetings. Jeff showed how he replaced two of five weekly standups with a daily brief that runs in Claude Cowork. Ben built a daily meeting prep skill live, in about ten minutes. This post walks through all four with enough detail that you can copy any of them this week. What is the Grain Claude connector? The Grain Claude connector is a one-click integration that lets Claude access your Grain meeting data through MCP (Model Context Protocol). Once installed, Claude can pull transcripts, notes, action items, and clips from any meeting you have access to in Grain. You install it once in Claude's connector directory, sign in with your Grain account, and Claude reads your meetings on demand inside any chat, skill, or scheduled task. It's the thing that makes the four workflows below possible without manual exports. Why meetings are the right context layer Before we walk through the workflows, a quick note on why all four start with meetings. Ben put it cleanly: "The challenge with one-off tasks and workflows is they're one-off. They don't have the context that we sometimes need. Whereas when we add that context layer, which we believe comes from meetings, ... we're unable to unlock even more richer content." Mike said something similar, but with a longer arc: "I started another company eight years ago and had this vision ... meeting data is the most underutilized asset that companies are sleeping on. This was in 2018. And now, with large language models, that original vision is finally being realized in ways I didn't even imagine were possible." The practical version: customer pushback, internal decisions, what someone actually committed to in standup. Most of that lives in calls. Almost none of it makes it into Notion, Linear, or HubSpot. Agents that can read your meetings stop guessing. Workflow 1: Mike's AI knowledge vault What it is: A Claude Code workflow that ingests meeting transcripts and documents into a personal knowledge graph, then uses that graph as context to generate work products like sales decks, marketing assets, and strategy memos. Inspired by: A tweet from Andrej Karpathy about treating Claude Code as a knowledge graph. The folder structure Vault/ ├── CLAUDE.md # tells Claude how to traverse the vault ├── Raw/ # dump everything here (meeting transcripts, docs, notes) ├── Wiki/ # Claude organizes Raw into a queryable knowledge base └── Output/ # Claude generates work products using the Wiki Three folders. One file. That's the whole foundation. How it runs A small server listens for Grain webhooks and drops new meeting transcripts into Raw/ automatically. Mike runs a compile skill in Claude Code. It processes new content in Raw/ , organizes it into the Wiki/ , and connects new topics to existing ones. When Mike needs to build something, he asked Claude to use the Wiki/ as context. Claude saves the output to Output/. He uses Claude Code hooks (pre-tool-use, post-tool-use) so Claude reads the Wiki/ at the start of every new session. The master index of the Wiki/ is 56 lines long. That's all Claude needs to know how to traverse the rest. What it produces The slides Ben presented during the webinar came out of this workflow. So did the sales deck Mike was about to present to a prospect an hour after the session ended. Mike's framing: "This whole thing started really, really simple. It started with just a CLAUDE.md file. It basically has three folders. Raw, Wiki, and Output. The Wiki is the knowledge graph that ultimately results from all of that." His next step is a team-level version: a shared voice-of-the-customer vault built from sales calls, intercom messages, support emails, and CRM data. Why this is worth copying It scales with your meetings. The more calls you have, the better the Wiki/ gets. The better the Wiki/ gets, the better every downstream output becomes. No manual prompt engineering after setup. Workflow 2: Mike's Slack alignment workflow What it is: A trigger-based Claude workflow that combines Grain MCP, Slack MCP, Amplitude MCP, and Figma to resolve internal disagreements with the right meeting clip, the right product data, and the right design artifact. Mike used this the day before the webinar to resolve a real misalignment with his team. The five-step flow Mike opened the Slack thread where there was a disagreement. He asked Claude to find the meeting where the original decision was discussed. Claude searched Grain via MCP, found the meeting (three months old), and created a clip of the relevant moment. Mike asked Claude to back the point up with product data. Claude queried Amplitude via MCP and pulled the relevant numbers. Mike asked Claude to check the related Figma files for additional context. Claude drafted the Slack reply with the clip embedded, the product data summarized, and the Figma references linked. Mike's framing: "It went through, did all of that work, analyzed the data, and then generated some reports. Where should all of this work go? Should we go put it in the Slack channel? Should we send a DM? Now that we have a strong conclusion, where do we want to close this workflow loop?" Why this is worth copying Most teams have these moments every week. Disagreements that would resolve instantly if someone could find the right meeting clip, the right metric, and the right design artifact. That used to take 30+ minutes of digging across tools. With the right MCPs connected, it takes a single prompt. Workflow 3: Jeff's Engineering Daily Brief What it is: A scheduled Claude task that pulls Linear, Slack, and Grain standup transcripts every morning to produce an engineering daily brief delivered as a Slack DM canvas. Jeff built this in Claude Cowork . It replaced two of his five weekly standups. What it pulls Linear: daily ticket movement (started, completed, blocked) Slack: engineering channel discussions from the last 24 hours Grain: transcripts from the three standups that still happen Persistent markdown file: the previous day's brief, so context carries forward What it produces A scannable summary of what moved, what's stuck, and what's waiting on a decision Accountability flags where commitments and delivery diverge. Not punitive. Jeff explicitly framed it that way. Positive shout-outs for things shipped A pinned canvas in his Slack DM with the full long-form brief A short summary DM that links to the canvas Jeff's framing: "I think a lot of times in companies, leaders use standups as a way to serve themselves and not necessarily serve the team. At Grain, for example, we only have three standups a week. And this is a way for me to keep up with what's going on without necessarily having a daily 30-minute meeting just to meet my needs." Why this is worth copying Daily standups are often a tax. A leader-targeted daily brief, generated automatically from data you already have, gives the leader what they need without forcing the whole team into a meeting. Jeff has about 12 recurring tasks running in Claude Cowork. This is one of them. Workflow 4: Ben's Daily Meeting Prep skill What it is: A Claude Cowork skill that runs every morning, pulls today's Google Calendar, searches Grain for past recordings with the same attendees, and posts a structured prep brief to a private Slack channel. Build time: About 10 minutes, live on screen during the webinar. The prompt Ben used to build it ‍ Build a daily meeting prep skill that runs each morning and does the following: - Pulls today 's meetings from my Google Calendar - Filters for events with external attendees - For each meeting, searches Grain for past recordings with the same attendees - Creates clips of relevant moments from those past calls - Writes a structured brief per meeting: themes, action items, follow-ups, one-sentence prep notes, past calls referenced - Posts the full brief to my private Slack channel as a daily message - Keeps each meeting in its own clearly separated section Claude Cowork asked clarifying questions (which Slack channel? what time? how to format clips?). Ben answered them inline. The skill saved. Now it can run every morning. Ben's framing: "Honestly, I iterated to this prompt with Claude itself. I didn't even write all this. I'm just giving structure for how simple it is to build one of these skills in Claude Cowork." Why this is worth copying Meeting prep is one of the highest-ROI uses of meeting context. If you have a 9 AM call with a customer you spoke to two months ago, you want the relevant clips, the open action items, and the last commitment surfaced before you join. This skill does that automatically. The pattern across all four Workflow Trigger Context source Output destination Mike's AI knowledge vault New meeting webhook Grain transcripts Local file in Output/ Mike's Slack alignment Manual prompt Grain + Slack + Amplitude + Figma Slack thread Jeff's daily brief Scheduled (daily AM) Linear + Slack + Grain standups Slack DM canvas Ben's meeting prep Scheduled (daily AM) Google Calendar + Grain Slack private channel Three things they share: Output lives in tools where work already happens. Slack, Linear, local files. No new app to open. Meeting context is in every one. Even the workflows that pull from Linear, Slack, or Amplitude all use Grain transcripts as the foundation. They all started simple. Mike's vault "started with just a CLAUDE.md file." Ben built his in 10 minutes. Jeff iterated his over weeks. The 4 levels of AI execution (Jeff's framework) Jeff laid out four levels of AI execution during the session. They map directly to how these workflows evolved. One-off tasks. "Help me draft this follow-up email." Useful, but doesn't compound. Reusable skills. Write a clear instruction set once, save it, run it on a new input. Scheduled workflows. A skill that runs on a cadence (daily, weekly) without you triggering it. Trigger-based workflows. A skill that runs when something happens. A meeting ends. A ticket moves. A webhook fires. Most teams are stuck at level 1. The leverage starts at level 2. Jeff's daily brief is a level 3. Ben's meeting prep is a level 3. Mike's vault is a level 4 (Grain webhooks trigger the sync). Mike's Slack alignment workflow is somewhere between 1 and 4 depending on how he runs it. You don't need to start at level 4. Levels 2 and 3 already create leverage most teams don't have. Tabi's reminder: you don't need to be technical The most quietly important moment of the session came at the end, from Thomas Tabi, Grain's Customer Success Lead: "I am not that technical, but I get Claude to do whatever I want. I just get in there, tell it what I want, and then try it out. So please don't feel like you need to be extremely technical to do anything. The key is: know what you want, then explore it in Claude, and you'll build a skill for you. No intimidation. Just tell it what you want." Every workflow above involves things that sound technical. Webhooks. MCPs. Hooks. Scheduled tasks. Folder structures. None of them required Tabi-level writing skill in those topics to start. Mike's vault started with a single CLAUDE.md file. Ben built his skill in Claude Cowork by writing a plain-English prompt that Claude turned into a working skill. Jeff iterated his daily brief by reading the output, telling Claude what was wrong, and letting Claude fix it. If you can explain what you want in plain language, you can build any of these. That's the practical version of Tabi's point. What to try this week Pick one workflow. Don't try to build all four at once. New to Claude + Grain? Start with Ben's daily meeting prep skill . Simplest setup, broadest payoff. You'll have it running in 15 minutes. Leader trying to reduce standups? Start with Jeff's daily brief . First version doesn't have to read all your sources. Start with Linear + Slack, add Grain when you're ready. Power user? Steal Mike's vault structure . Three folders, a CLAUDE.md , a compile skill. Build the rest as you go. Not technical? Re-read Tabi's quote above. Then start anyway. Frequently asked questions What is the Grain Claude connector? The Grain Claude connector is a one-click integration that lets Claude access your Grain meeting data through MCP. Once installed, Claude can pull transcripts, notes, action items, and clips on demand from any meeting you have access to in Grain. What can the Grain MCP do? The Grain MCP supports fetching meetings, transcripts, notes, and action items. It can also create clips of specific moments and generate playlists that group multiple meetings under a single shareable link. Do I need an enterprise Claude plan to use the Grain connector? No. You can use the Grain MCP on any Grain plan. For scheduled and trigger-based workflows, you'll want Claude Pro, Team, or Enterprise so you have access to Claude Cowork. What is Claude Cowork? Claude Cowork is Claude's feature for scheduled and recurring tasks. You define a task once (e.g., "every morning, build me a meeting prep brief"), and Claude runs it on a schedule. Both Jeff's daily brief and Ben's meeting prep skill run in Claude Cowork. How do I make a Claude workflow run automatically when a meeting ends? Use Grain webhooks (via the Grain API) or the Grain Zapier integration. Both expose triggers like "meeting finished" and "meeting uploaded." Connect that trigger to a Claude workflow via the Zapier SDK or a small custom server, and the workflow runs the moment a meeting wraps. Can the Grain Claude connector access my coworkers' private meetings? No. Each person connects the Grain MCP to their own Grain account. The connector only accesses meetings that you personally have access to in Grain. What's the difference between a scheduled workflow and a trigger-based workflow? Scheduled workflows run on a fixed cadence (e.g., every weekday at 8 AM). Trigger-based workflows run when an event happens (e.g., a meeting ends, a ticket moves to "complete"). Scheduled workflows are easier to build. Trigger-based workflows respond faster to real-world events. How long does it take to build one of these AI workflows? Ben built his daily meeting prep skill live during the webinar in about 10 minutes. Jeff's engineering daily brief took longer because he iterated on the structure over several weeks. Mike's knowledge vault started as a single CLAUDE.md file and grew over months. Do I need to be technical to build AI workflows with Grain and Claude? No. As Thomas Tabi (Grain's Customer Success Lead) put it during the session: "I am not that technical, but I get Claude to do whatever I want." If you can explain what you want a workflow to do in plain English, Claude can help you build it. You don't need to write code. Resources Watch the full session (60 min) Connect Grain to Claude If you build one of these for yourself, we'd love to hear about it. We've started spotlighting customers who are building real workflows on top of Grain. Reach out.

title: Socratix AI Raises $4.1M to Empower Fraud Fighters with AI
summary: Socratix AI announces $4.1M seed funding led by Pear VC to build autonomous AI coworkers for fraud and risk teams.
body_text: The seed round, led by Pear VC, will accelerate the team building autonomous AI coworkers for fraud and risk operations. The announcement Socratix AI , the company building autonomous AI coworkers for fraud and risk teams, announced a $4.1 million seed round led by Pear VC , with participation from Y Combinator , Twenty Two Ventures, Transpose Platform Management, and a group of strategic angel investors. The funding will accelerate hiring across engineering and go-to-market teams, expand participation in fraud and risk industry organizations, and support ongoing product research and development. $4.1M seed financing Pear VC round lead 2025 announced Why now Fraudsters are exploiting automation, synthetic identities, and generative AI to overwhelm outdated defenses. At the same time, analysts remain bogged down in manual investigations, siloed data, and costly judgment calls. “ Fraud analysts are drowning in manual work while fraudsters are scaling with AI. We're building AI coworkers that take on the repetitive investigation work, so analysts can focus on the judgment calls that protect financial systems and customer trust. Riya Jagetia CEO and Co-Founder, Socratix AI Built from experience Socratix is building this new operating model through experience earned on the front lines. title: 11 best ServiceTitan competitors in 2026
summary: Your comprehensive guide to the top ServiceTitan alternatives to assess if you’re a prospective first-time customer or considering switching.
body_text: An established home services company with dozens of technicians and a five-person residential service company have one thing in common: both businesses need field service software. But they don’t necessarily need the same platform. ServiceTitan can run nearly every aspect of your contracting business — which is exactly why it works so well for some teams and feels like too much software for others. The best ServiceTitan alternative depends on: The type and quantity of work you do The size of your team The systems you already use Your business’s operational complexity This guide is designed for home services contractors who are looking to invest in a CRM or switch to a new one. We compare 11 of the leading ServiceTitan competitors, diving deep into their features, pricing, pros, and cons to help you pinpoint which platform is right for your business. ‍ ServiceTitan alternatives at a glance ‍ Platform Best for Standout strength Pricing approach ServiceTitan Established contractors with larger or more complex operations Broad field service and business management capabilities Per-technician custom pricing Jobber Small service businesses Ease of use Published tiered plans Housecall Pro Residential home services Mobile tools and payments Published tiered plans Service Fusion Budget-conscious teams Unlimited-user pricing Flat-rate tiers FieldEdge HVAC and plumbing contractors QuickBooks integration Custom pricing Workiz Phone-driven service businesses Call tracking and dispatch Tiered plans FieldPulse Growing contractors Flexible workflows Configured or custom pricing BuildOps Commercial contractors Commercial operations management Custom pricing ServiceTrade Commercial service and maintenance Asset and recurring-service management Team-based custom pricing Simpro Complex, multi-location businesses Inventory and job costing Custom pricing Salesforce Field Service Enterprise organizations Customization and CRM connectivity Per-user pricing Acculynx Roofing contractors Roofing-specific CRM and job management Starts at $250/month; custom pricing for higher plans ‍ This summary reflects each company’s current product details and pricing as of August 2026. Pricing and plan availability can change, so confirm current costs directly with each provider. ‍ A quick overview of ServiceTitan To understand how the alternatives compare, start with what ServiceTitan is built to handle and where it fits best. ‍ What ServiceTitan does ServiceTitan is an all-in-one field service management platform for residential and commercial contractors . It connects virtually all of the work that happens between generating a lead and getting a customer’s first call through the final payment, including: Marketing Call booking Scheduling and dispatch Customer relationship management Estimates and proposals Invoicing and payments Financing Pricebook management Technician mobile workflows Inventory and purchasing Payroll and commission tracking Marketing attribution Reporting and dashboards ServiceTitan prices its packages per technician and offers different feature tiers. For exact rates, you’ll need to request a quote directly from ServiceTitan. ‍ Who typically uses ServiceTitan? ServiceTitan is primarily used by established trade businesses in fields like HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and roofing. Its platform supports residential and commercial service, as well as construction workflows. Growing contractors typically turn to ServiceTitan when separate scheduling, accounting, sales, and reporting tools can no longer keep up with the business. ServiceTitan gives the office and field a shared operating system, with enough depth to support larger teams and more structured processes. ‍ Is ServiceTitan a CRM or ERP? ServiceTitan includes a CRM, but it does far more than just store customer records and sales activity. Think of ServiceTitan as a field service management (FSM) and business operations platform. For some contractors, its job costing, purchasing, reporting, payroll, and inventory features can perform many ERP-like functions. Businesses with more complicated financial requirements may still pair it with a dedicated ERP (enterprise resource planning) or accounting system . ‍ What you should know before choosing ServiceTitan ServiceTitan offers a long list of useful features, but that doesn’t automatically mean it’ll be the right fit for your business. Before choosing ServiceTitan, consider: How much the full implementation will cost How long onboarding and configuration will take Whether employees will use the platform consistently Which advanced features your team will actually use How it connects with your accounting and operational tools Who will own the system internally How much reporting depth you need Whether the platform fits where your business is heading ‍ 👉 For a deeper look at the platform, read our complete guide to ServiceTitan . ‍ Why consider a ServiceTitan alternative? ServiceTitan is one of the biggest names in field service software, so it’s likely to come up early in your search. That doesn’t mean it should be the only platform you look at though. If you’re investing in your first field service system, comparing competitors helps you understand what you actually need. For example, small teams might prefer something easier to set up, while an established commercial service business might care more about project management or recurring maintenance. And some teams might just want clearer pricing and fewer moving parts. And if you’re a current ServiceTitan user who’s considering switching, it helps to understand what’s actually available to you before you move on. It’s worth comparing ServiceTitan alternatives when: You’re shopping for your first field service platform and want a clearer view of the market. Your team needs a faster, lighter implementation. ServiceTitan has more bells and whistles than your business needs. Pricing feels difficult to predict. Another platform is better suited to your trade or business model. You need stronger project, inventory, or asset management. Your team is struggling to use ServiceTitan consistently. You’re paying for features that you rarely or never use. A side-by-side comparison makes it easier to see where ServiceTitan is a strong fit and where another platform may better suit your business. ‍ How we chose the best ServiceTitan competitors We don’t take product recommendations and reviews lightly. To bring you this list of ServiceTitan competitors, we compared each platform based on the factors that affect daily use and long-term value: Industries and company sizes served Scheduling and dispatch CRM and customer communication Estimates, invoices, and payments Technician mobile experience Reporting and analytics Inventory and job costing Call management and marketing tools Integrations Implementation requirements Pricing structure and transparency Ability to support growth Common limitations You’ll notice we didn’t select one single “best overall” winner. That’s because field service software isn’t one-size-fits-all. The right choice comes down to your needs, and overall fit is more important than feature count. ‍ ServiceTitan review ServiceTitan is arguably the industry’s most popular software. Built for residential and commercial contractors, ServiceTitan has a solution for every part of the job cycle, designed to help your business win more contracts, speed up work flows, increase productivity, and grow revenue. ServiceTitan’s depth and comprehensive offerings are its biggest draw, especially for established contractors with larger teams or more complicated operations. But with that comes more extensive setup and training requirements, plus a steeper learning curve than a lighter-weight platform. Pricing ServiceTitan uses a per-technician pricing model and doesn’t publish dollar amounts. It currently offers three core packages: Starter, Essentials, and The Works , with additional Pro products available separately. You’ll need to request a quote for exact pricing. Key features Scheduling and dispatch Call booking CRM and customer management Estimates and invoicing Pricebook management Payroll and commission tracking Advanced reporting and dashboards Service agreements Inventory and job costing Mobile tools for technicians Marketing tools and attribution Commercial service and construction workflows ‍ Pros Cons Extensive feature set can replace several disconnected tools May be more software than a small or straightforward business needs Supports residential service, commercial service, and construction Pricing isn’t publicly available, making upfront cost comparisons harder Strong reporting and operational visibility Getting full value may require proper setup, training, and ongoing system ownership Built to support larger and more complex contractor operations Per-technician pricing means costs can increase as the field team grows 70+ pre-built integrations extend the platform into other business systems Some advanced capabilities are only available in higher packages or separate Pro products ‍ 11 ServiceTitan alternatives worth considering ‍ 1. Jobber: Best for small service businesses Jobber is built for small and midsize service companies that want to manage customer records, quotes, scheduling, invoicing, and payments without an overwhelming implementation process. Jobber’s Client Hub gives you one place to approve quotes, check appointment details, pay invoices, and request more work. Jobber also offers job-costing and profitability tools, although its reporting and operational controls are generally less extensive than ServiceTitan’s. Pricing Jobber currently publishes three plans ranging from $29 to $149 per month when billed annually, with plans designed for solo operators through larger and multi-location teams. Core: $149/month Connect: $99/month Grow: $29/month Key features Scheduling and dispatch Customer CRM Quotes and invoices Online booking Client portal Automated reminders Online payments Job profitability reporting Mobile app ‍ Pros Cons Straightforward onboarding Less depth for large, complicated operations Accessible interface Fewer enterprise controls Published pricing Reporting may become limiting as the business grows Strong customer-facing tools Good fit for smaller teams ‍ How Jobber compares with ServiceTitan Jobber prioritizes a shorter learning curve and easier day-to-day management, while ServiceTitan provides more advanced reporting, marketing, call booking, payroll, and operational tools. Jobber is likely the better fit when you want to get up and running quickly. ServiceTitan becomes more compelling as your business adds technicians, departments, locations, and management layers. ‍ 2. Housecall Pro: Best for residential service businesses that want a simpler setup Housecall Pro is designed for residential service companies that need scheduling, dispatch, estimates, payments, financing, and customer communication in one system. Its mobile experience and customer-facing tools make it especially relevant for teams that spend most of the day moving between short residential jobs. Housecall Pro positions itself as a platform for companies ranging from solo operators to teams with more than 100 people. Pricing Housecall Pro’s pricing starts at $59 per month, but costs vary by plan, users, and added capabilities. They promote three plans*: Basic: Approximately $79/month Essentials: Approximately $229/month Max: Approximately $350/month *These prices are for individual users, not plans for teams. Key features Scheduling and dispatch Online booking Estimates and invoices Customer notifications Pricebook Payments Consumer financing Service plans Marketing tools Technician mobile app ‍ Pros Cons Fast setup Add-ons can increase the total price Strong mobile workflows Reporting may not match ServiceTitan’s depth Useful payment and financing options Less suited to highly customized enterprise operations Accessible for smaller businesses Good customer communication features ‍ How Housecall Pro compares with ServiceTitan Housecall Pro covers many of the core workflows a residential contractor needs without demanding the same implementation effort. ServiceTitan offers more control when you need sophisticated reporting, call-center workflows, inventory management, and marketing attribution. ‍ 3. Service Fusion: Best for predictable, unlimited-user pricing Service Fusion is a field service management platform for small and midsize contractors. It handles the core work of scheduling jobs, dispatching technicians, managing customers, creating estimates, sending invoices, and collecting payments. Unlike platforms that charge per user or technician, Service Fusion offers unlimited users for a flat monthly price, which makes costs easier to predict as your office and field teams grow. Pricing Service Fusion’s official pricing page promotes three plans: Starter, Plus, and Pro. Pricing is not made publicly available, so you’ll need to request a quote from Service Fusion directly. Key features Customer management Scheduling and dispatch Estimates and jobs Invoicing and payments QuickBooks integration Inventory management Job costing GPS fleet tracking Reporting Customer portal Recurring invoicing ‍ Pros Cons Unlimited users The interface may feel less modern than some newer platforms Flat monthly pricing Reporting may not match ServiceTitan’s depth Broad core feature set Reporting and customization may be less advanced Potentially good value for teams with many users Smaller partner ecosystem than ServiceTitan ‍ How Service Fusion compares with ServiceTitan Service Fusion offers a more predictable cost structure than ServiceTitan. ServiceTitan brings deeper analytics, marketing, payroll, and revenue-management capabilities, but its per-technician pricing can produce a very different cost profile as the team grows. ‍ 4. FieldEdge: Best for HVAC and plumbing businesses using QuickBooks FieldEdge is built for field service companies, with a particularly strong presence in HVAC and plumbing. The platform connects scheduling, dispatch, customer records, service agreements, pricing, invoicing, and technician workflows. Its QuickBooks integration is a major part of the product’s positioning, making it relevant for contractors who don’t want to replace their accounting system. Pricing FieldEdge’s official pricing page promotes three plans: Select, Premier, and Elite. Pricing is not made publicly available, so you’ll need to request a quote from FieldEdge directly. Key features Scheduling and dispatch Customer and service history Estimates and invoices Service agreements Pricebook management Payments Performance reporting QuickBooks Online and Desktop integrations Technician mobile app ‍ Pros Cons Built around trade contractor workflows Pricing is not published Strong accounting connection Some buyers may prefer a more modern interface Established HVAC and plumbing focus Marketing and analytics are less extensive in some areas Familiar feature set for ServiceTitan users ‍ How FieldEdge compares with ServiceTitan FieldEdge may be a better fit for contractors that want HVAC or plumbing operations software tied closely to QuickBooks. ServiceTitan is broader, particularly for businesses that want marketing attribution, advanced reporting, and more functions inside one platform. ‍ 5. Workiz: Best for service businesses that rely on inbound calls For some service companies, the phone is still the center of the revenue engine. A missed call can mean a lost job before the dispatcher ever opens the schedule. Workiz combines field service management with a built-in phone and communications system. It empowers your team to track calls, record conversations, connect lead sources to booked jobs, and manage customer communication alongside scheduling and dispatch. Pricing Workiz offers three plans: Standard, Pro, and Ultimate. Pricing isn’t publicly available, and costs are based on the package, number of users, and selected features. Key features Built-in phone system Call tracking and recording Lead management Scheduling and dispatch Estimates and invoices Online booking Automated messaging Equipment tracking Payments Mobile app ‍ Pros Cons Strong phone and call-tracking capabilities Less depth for complex enterprise operations Useful for businesses with heavy inbound lead volume Inventory and commercial project workflows may be more limited Connects communication with job records Phone and advanced features can affect the final price Accessible interface ‍ How Workiz compares with ServiceTitan Both Workiz and ServiceTitan can connect calls to operational outcomes. Workiz makes its integrated communications system a central part of the product, while ServiceTitan offers a wider range of management, reporting, marketing, and enterprise capabilities. ‍ 6. FieldPulse: Best for growing teams that want flexible workflows FieldPulse sits somewhere in between scheduling software and larger enterprise platforms. It brings scheduling, CRM, estimates, invoices, custom forms, project management, inventory, time tracking, and technician tools into one field service system. Its flexible setup can appeal to contractors that need more control but aren’t ready for the cost or implementation requirements of ServiceTitan. Pricing FieldPulse provides an online pricing tool rather than a single universal starting price. Cost depends on your team size and desired field service capabilities. They offer three plans: Essential, Professional, and Enterprise. Key features Scheduling and dispatch CRM Estimates and invoicing Custom forms Project management Inventory Time tracking Technician management Mobile access ‍ Pros Cons Configurable workflows Smaller integration ecosystem than larger competitors Modern user experience Less depth in advanced marketing and reporting Broad functionality for growing teams Pricing may require configuration or a sales conversation Bridges the gap between basic and enterprise software ‍ How FieldPulse compares with ServiceTitan If your contracting business is growing, FieldPulse can give you more room to shape workflows without taking on the full weight of ServiceTitan. ServiceTitan remains stronger for businesses that need mature analytics, revenue tools, and extensive operational controls. ‍ 7. BuildOps: Best for commercial contractors A lot of field service platforms began with residential workflows and later expanded into commercial work. BuildOps took the opposite approach. BuildOps was designed from the get-go for commercial contractors managing service, projects, assets, field teams, finances, and customer relationships. Its focus includes mechanical, HVAC, electrical, plumbing, and other specialty trades working on commercial buildings. Pricing BuildOps doesn’t publish standard subscription prices. Pricing is customized to the organization and the capabilities you need. Key features Commercial dispatch Project management Asset and equipment tracking CRM Proposals and invoicing Job costing Technician mobile tools Reporting Customer portal ‍ Pros Cons Strong commercial focus Greater implementation commitment Supports service and project work Custom pricing Connects assets, properties, customers, and jobs Likely excessive for small residential businesses Suitable for larger operations ‍ How BuildOps compares with ServiceTitan BuildOps is built around the complexity of commercial contracting. ServiceTitan supports commercial operations too, but you’ll want to carefully compare how each platform handles project work, asset history, billing structures, and field service requirements. ‍ 8. ServiceTrade: Best for recurring commercial service and maintenance ServiceTrade is designed for commercial contractors managing recurring service agreements, inspections, maintenance visits, repairs, and equipment histories. Its platform is especially relevant to mechanical and fire protection contractors. Inspection workflows, deficiency tracking, asset records, and digital documentation help teams manage work where compliance and recurring service drive the customer relationship. Pricing ServiceTrade prices its platform based on team size. They offer three plans: Select, Premium, and Enterprise. You'll need to contact the company for a specific quote. Key features Asset tracking Recurring service agreements Scheduling and dispatch Inspection workflows Deficiency tracking Technician mobile tools Customer portal Quotes and invoices Service reporting ‍ Pros Cons Strong recurring-service workflows Less focused on residential sales Detailed asset histories May not replace every accounting or back-office platform Good fit for inspection-heavy commercial contractors Requires custom implementation and pricing Supports compliance documentation ‍ How ServiceTrade compares with ServiceTitan ServiceTrade goes deep on commercial maintenance, inspections, and asset-based service. ServiceTitan offers broader business management capabilities and may be more attractive to contractors who balance residential and commercial work. ‍ 9. Simpro: Best for complex, multi-location field service operations Simpro is built for contractors managing service calls, projects, inventory, purchasing, job costs, assets, and field crews across a more complicated operation. It supports recurring maintenance and short service jobs alongside multi-stage projects and progress billing. Simpro also positions the platform for teams ranging from small businesses to multi-region enterprises with hundreds of employees. Pricing Simpro uses custom pricing based on the business and required products. Customers can sign up for the base plan, then pay for specific add-ons as desired. You’ll need to request a custom quote from Simpro. Key features Scheduling and dispatch Project management Inventory and purchasing Job costing Asset maintenance Recurring work Progress billing Reporting Mobile field tools Multi-region support ‍ Pros Cons Strong inventory and job-costing capabilities Steeper learning curve Handles both service and project work More involved implementation Supports operational complexity May be too complex for smaller contractors Suitable for multi-location contractors ‍ How Simpro compares with ServiceTitan Simpro is a serious option for businesses where inventory, project work, purchasing, and job profitability sit at the center of operations. ServiceTitan may have the advantage for residential sales, call handling, marketing, and customer-facing revenue workflows. ‍ 10. Salesforce Field Service: Best for enterprises already using Salesforce Salesforce Field Service extends Salesforce into field operations. The platform connects work orders, cases, customer accounts, assets, scheduling, dispatch, contractors, and mobile employees. Its biggest advantage is its ability to configure field service around a broader Salesforce environment. Pricing Salesforce currently lists Dispatcher and Technician licenses at $175 per user per month when billed annually. Contractor licenses range from $55 to $80 per month, while broader bundles cost more. Field Service also requires qualifying Salesforce licenses, which must be included in the full cost comparison. Key features Work order management Asset management Appointment booking Scheduling and optimization Dispatcher console Service contracts Mobile tools Inventory and product tracking CRM analytics Salesforce integrations ‍ Pros Cons Extensive customization Complex implementation Strong CRM connection Licensing and customization costs can add up Broad app and partner ecosystem Less purpose-built for home services out of the box Suitable for complex enterprise environments ‍ How Salesforce Field Service compares with ServiceTitan Salesforce Field Service is the stronger candidate when Salesforce already serves as your central CRM and data platform. ServiceTitan requires less construction from scratch because it comes with workflows designed specifically for the trades. ‍ 11. Acculynx: Best for roofing contractors who need a CRM AccuLynx is built specifically for roofing contractors, which gives it a much narrower focus than most of the field service platforms on this list. It combines a CRM and sales platform with estimating, material ordering, production management, job tracking, and financial management tools. Acculynx’s roofing focus is its biggest advantage. Measurements from providers like EagleView, HOVER, Geospan, and GAF QuickMeasure can feed directly into estimates, while integrations with suppliers like ABC Supply, SRS Distribution, and QXO let roofers access product catalogs and preferred pricing from within AccuLynx. Pricing Acculynx offers three plans: Essential, Pro, and Elite. The Essential plan starts at $250/month. For Pro and Elite plan pricing, you’ll need to request a custom quote from Acculynx. Key features Roofing CRM and lead management Estimates, contracts, and e-signatures Aerial measurement integrations Material calculations and supplier ordering Scheduling and job tracking Production and workflow management Job photos and document management Invoicing and financial tools Custom reporting Mobile field app ‍ Pros Cons Built specifically for roofing workflows Narrower fit for contractors who work across multiple trades Connects roofing measurements directly to estimates Advanced workflow and multi-location features require the Elite plan Direct ordering from major roofing suppliers Less oriented around high-volume service and dispatch operations than ServiceTitan Covers both sales and production workflows ‍ How Acculynx compares with ServiceTitan The biggest difference between Acculynx and ServiceTitan is scope. AccuLynx was designed around the roofing job lifecycle. ServiceTitan supports roofing too, but it’s built for a much broader range of home service trades and puts more emphasis on service operations like call booking, dispatch, technician management, and recurring service. If you’re a roofing contractor who primarily wants a CRM built around how roofers sell and manage projects, AccuLynx is worth a close look. ‍ Which ServiceTitan alternative is right for your business? ‍ Business summary Platforms to consider Why Solo operator or very small team Jobber, Housecall Pro Easier setup and simpler workflows Growing residential contractor Housecall Pro, FieldPulse, FieldEdge More operational depth without a full enterprise system Established residential contractor with a larger field team ServiceTitan, FieldEdge Deeper dispatch, reporting, sales, and operational capabilities Budget-conscious team with many users Service Fusion Unlimited-user pricing Phone-heavy service business Workiz, ServiceTitan Strong tools for connecting inbound calls, leads, bookings, and job outcomes HVAC or plumbing company using QuickBooks FieldEdge Trade focus and accounting connection Commercial mechanical contractor BuildOps, ServiceTrade, ServiceTitan Commercial projects, assets, and recurring service Complex multi-location contractor Simpro, ServiceTitan Inventory, job costing, and operational controls Salesforce-based enterprise Salesforce Field Service Deep CRM and workflow customization Roofing contractors Acculynx Built specifically around roofing workflows ‍ What to look for in a ServiceTitan alternative ‍ Fit for your trade and business model Start with how your company makes money. Residential service businesses need fast booking, efficient dispatch, clear proposals, and easy payment collection. Commercial contractors may care more about assets, contracts, inspections, project costing, and complex billing. Consider whether the platform is designed for: Residential or commercial work Service calls or long-term projects One-time jobs or recurring maintenance Sales-driven or asset-driven operations A platform built for the wrong model will never be a good fit no matter how many features it includes. ‍ Ease of adoption There’s no use investing in software if no one uses it, or it doesn’t make your work easier. A powerful platform with weak adoption is just an expensive place to store data. Assess the user experience for dispatchers, CSRs, managers, and technicians. Find out how long implementation takes, what training is included, and how much work you’ll need to do to configure the system to your needs. ‍ Total cost, not just the subscription The monthly subscription fee is only one line in the budget. Calculate the cost of: Implementation Data migration Add-ons Payment processing Integrations Training Support Internal administration Lost productivity during rollout A less expensive subscription can still become a costly move if the migration is difficult or you need several add-ons to recreate its current workflow. ‍ Reporting and operational visibility Reporting should help you run the business, not force you into another data-cleaning project. Test whether the platform can clearly show: Booking rates Technician productivity Job profitability Revenue Marketing performance Capacity Outstanding work Customer retention Confirm that the system uses the same definitions your company uses. A dashboard is only helpful if you can trust the numbers. ‍ Integrations with your current systems Your field service platform needs to work with any accounting, payroll, financing, communications, inventory, or other operational tools you use. ‍ 👉 ServiceTitan integrates with PermitFlow, empowering you to connect your field service operation with dedicated permitting and inspections management . ‍ Ability to support future growth Buy for the business you expect to become, but don’t ignore the team you have today. Think two or three years ahead. More technicians, locations, trades, and jurisdictions can change what your business needs from its software. At the same time, it is possible to overbuy. The most sophisticated system on the market has little value if your employees avoid it because every basic task takes too long. ‍ Is it worth switching from ServiceTitan? Switching from ServiceTitan to a new CRM or field service management system might be worthwhile, but the ongoing problem needs to be substantial enough to justify the disruption. Here’s what to consider before switching: ‍ Your main concern What to consider before switching Price Compare annual savings with migration, retraining, and add-on costs Low adoption Determine whether the problem is the platform, configuration, or training Missing features Confirm that another system closes the gap without creating new ones Reporting problems Check whether configuration, integrations, or new dashboards could solve them Poor workflow fit Replacement may make sense when workarounds have become standard procedure Greater business complexity Compare commercial or enterprise platforms against future requirements ‍ How hard is it to switch from ServiceTitan? Your field service platform will be holding years of operational history, so replacing it is more than transferring a customer list. Keep in mind that the migration might involve: Exporting customer, job, and equipment records Cleaning and mapping data Rebuilding pricebooks Recreating forms and workflows Reconnecting integrations Retraining dispatchers, CSRs, managers, and technicians Running both systems in parallel Managing a temporary drop in productivity The larger the company and the more customized your ServiceTitan account, the more involved the move is likely to be. ‍ When switching makes sense Switching deserves serious consideration when: Employees consistently avoid the platform. Manual workarounds are affecting job execution. The business pays for substantial functionality it never uses. Another platform clearly fits the operating model better. The expected savings or performance gains justify the transition. Low adoption is especially important. Software can’t produce accurate reporting when the underlying data is missing, late, or inconsistent. ‍ When staying with ServiceTitan makes sense Staying may be the better decision when: You rely on ServiceTitan’s reporting, marketing, accounting, inventory, or financing tools. The platform is deeply embedded in your operations. Employees use it consistently. The business has invested heavily in configuration and automation. Problems can be fixed through training, process changes, or integrations. The cost of staying is easy to see on a software invoice. The cost of replacing a system that already works can be harder to spot until you’ve started migrating. ‍ Choose the platform that fits the way your business works There’s no universal winner if you’re looking for the best ServiceTitan alternative. At the end of the day, you have to compare the work, not the sales decks. Before you commit, look closely at how each option handles the work your team does every day. Test scheduling, dispatch, reporting, billing, and integrations using real workflows. Factor in implementation, training, and the ongoing effort required to keep the system running well. And remember, your field service platform doesn’t need to do everything itself. Specialized systems can fill the gaps without forcing your business to replace its operational foundation. For example, PermitFlow works alongside contractor software to handle permit research, preparation, submission, tracking, inspections, and closeouts. With PermitFlow, you’ll see a: 90% reduction in permitting overhead 2.5x faster permit approvals 5x return on investment Learn more about permit management with PermitFlow . ‍ FAQs Who are ServiceTitan’s biggest competitors? Major ServiceTitan competitors include Jobber, Housecall Pro, Service Fusion, FieldEdge, Workiz, FieldPulse, BuildOps, ServiceTrade, Simpro, and Salesforce Field Service. The closest competitor depends on the business. Jobber and Housecall Pro are common comparisons for smaller residential teams. BuildOps, ServiceTrade, and Simpro are more relevant to complex commercial operations. ‍ What is the best ServiceTitan alternative for a small business? Jobber and Housecall Pro are often recommended as the best ServiceTitan alternatives for small residential service businesses because they offer published pricing and cover core workflows without a massive implementation. Service Fusion may be worth considering if your growing team wants unlimited users and a flat monthly price. ‍ What is the best ServiceTitan alternative for commercial contractors? BuildOps, ServiceTrade, and Simpro are three leading options for commercial contractors. BuildOps supports commercial service and project operations. ServiceTrade is strong for recurring maintenance, assets, and inspections. Simpro fits businesses that need inventory, purchasing, job costing, and multi-stage project management. ‍ Is ServiceNow the same as ServiceTitan? No, they are separate companies and products. ServiceTitan is built for contractors and field service businesses. ServiceNow is a broader enterprise workflow platform known for IT service management, incident management, employee workflows, and other large-company processes. ‍ Who owns ServiceTitan? ServiceTitan, Inc. is a publicly traded company listed on Nasdaq under the ticker TTAN. It is owned by its shareholders rather than a private parent company. Ara Mahdessian serves as co-founder and CEO, while Vahe Kuzoyan is co-founder and president. ‍ What industries does ServiceTitan support besides HVAC and plumbing? ServiceTitan supports electrical, roofing, garage door, water treatment, irrigation, septic, painting, pool service, landscaping, lawn care, pest control, air duct cleaning, and other residential and commercial trades. Some industries may be served through products or companies within the broader ServiceTitan portfolio. ‍ When did ServiceTitan become popular with home service businesses? ServiceTitan was founded in 2012 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan. The company expanded quickly during the late 2010s as contractors looked for cloud-based alternatives to disconnected office and field systems. By 2019, ServiceTitan reported more than 2,500 client businesses, rising to more than 5,000 by the end of 2020. It’s now a public company serving residential and commercial contractors.

title: T-MEC 2026: la revisión que ya está reordenando la logística de Norteamérica antes de que se firme una sola línea
summary: El T-MEC 2026 aún se negocia, pero las cadenas de suministro ya se están moviendo. Conoce qué implica la revisión del tratado y cómo adelantarte a los cambios.
body_text: Sign in Welcome! Log into your account Forgot your password? Get help Password recovery Recover your password A password will be e-mailed to you. T-MEC 2026: la revisión que ya está reordenando la logística de Norteamérica antes de que se firme una sola línea Nadie espera al resultado final: proveedores, rutas y documentos comerciales ya se están moviendo. Esto es lo que la revisión del tratado está cambiando en el terreno operativo. Industria 13/08/2026 Todavía no hay un solo párrafo modificado en el T-MEC, pero en los pisos de producción, en las aduanas y en los centros de distribución de México, Estados Unidos y Canadá, algo ya cambió. La revisión programada para 2026 no ha concluido, y sin embargo las empresas dejaron de comportarse como si el tratado fuera un documento fijo. Lo tratan como un texto en movimiento, y eso las obliga a moverse con él. Es un fenómeno poco común en el comercio internacional: normalmente las compañías esperan a que un cambio regulatorio se publique para reaccionar. Esta vez, la sola posibilidad de que las reglas se endurezcan ya está costando dinero, tiempo y decisiones estratégicas. La incertidumbre, en la logística moderna, funciona como un costo más. El tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá vuelve a estar en el centro de la conversación El T-MEC nunca dejó de ser relevante, pero su revisión periódica lo puso otra vez bajo el reflector de gobiernos, cámaras empresariales y equipos de comercio exterior. Sobre la mesa hay temas que van más allá de aranceles: seguridad económica, dependencia de proveedores externos y, sobre todo, el fortalecimiento de las reglas de origen. Washington ha insistido en que el acuerdo debe beneficiar principalmente a la producción hecha en Norteamérica, no a mercancías que solo pasan por la región para aprovechar preferencias arancelarias. Esa postura, aunque todavía no se traduce en un texto legal modificado, ya funciona como una señal de alerta para cualquier empresa cuya cadena de suministro dependa de insumos asiáticos o de terceros mercados. El resultado es que muchas organizaciones están auditando, por primera vez en años, de dónde viene realmente cada componente de sus productos. No para cumplir con una norma nueva (que aún no existe), sino para no quedar expuestas si esa norma llega. En sectores como el automotriz o el electrónico, donde un solo producto puede reunir piezas de media docena de países, ese ejercicio de revisión implica meses de trabajo entre compras, producción y comercio exterior. Lo interesante es que este movimiento anticipado convierte a la negociación misma en un factor logístico. Ya no importa solo qué dice el tratado hoy, sino hacia dónde parece dirigirse la conversación entre los tres gobiernos. Implicaciones del Tratado de Libre Comercio para las cadenas de suministro Si el tratado se mueve, la logística también. Y las implicaciones ya son visibles en al menos cuatro frentes. La diversificación de proveedores dejó de ser un plan a futuro La regionalización de las cadenas de suministro venía avanzando desde la pandemia, pero la revisión del T-MEC le dio un nuevo empujón. No se trata de abandonar por completo a los proveedores asiáticos, sino de construir redes con más opciones: alternativas dentro de Norteamérica que permitan reaccionar rápido si las condiciones comerciales cambian. Eso obliga a rediseñar transporte, inventarios y centros de distribución pensando en flexibilidad, no solo en costo. La trazabilidad se volvió un activo estratégico, no un trámite Si el origen de las mercancías va a examinarse con más rigor, entonces cada certificado, cada registro de proveedor y cada movimiento de inventario cobra un peso distinto. El reto para los equipos de logística ya no es solo generar documentación, sino que esa información fluya sin fisuras entre áreas. Un dato inconsistente puede significar una inspección adicional, un retraso en frontera o, en el peor de los casos, la pérdida de beneficios arancelarios que llevaron años de trabajo conseguir. Gestionar riesgos ya pesa tanto como reducir costos Durante años, el desempeño logístico se midió casi exclusivamente por tiempos de entrega y tarifas de transporte. Ese estándar está cambiando. Hoy se valora también la capacidad de una cadena de suministro para absorber un golpe regulatorio sin detenerse: rutas alternas, mayor visibilidad de las operaciones, políticas de inventario menos ajustadas. La revisión del tratado no inventó esta tendencia, pero la aceleró de forma notoria. La integración regional gana terreno frente a la lógica global Más allá del texto técnico, el mensaje de fondo que dejan las negociaciones es claro: los tres países quieren cadenas de suministro más integradas entre sí y menos dependientes de proveedores externos. Eso abre una ventana para México como plataforma manufacturera y logística, siempre que la infraestructura, la eficiencia aduanera y la conectividad entre modos de transporte estén a la altura de esa ambición. Adaptarse antes de que termine la negociación Ninguna empresa puede esperar a que el T-MEC 2026 quede firmado para empezar a prepararse: para cuando eso ocurra, quienes ya ajustaron sus proveedores, blindaron su documentación y flexibilizaron sus rutas tendrán una ventaja difícil de alcanzar. La revisión del tratado todavía está en curso, pero el nuevo mapa logístico de Norteamérica ya se está dibujando, decisión por decisión, en cada empresa que decide no quedarse quieta mientras los gobiernos negocian. En ese sentido, el verdadero indicador a observar en los próximos meses no será únicamente el texto que finalmente se firme, sino la velocidad con la que la industria logística logre traducir la incertidumbre en estrategia. Quienes entiendan que la revisión del T-MEC es, sobre todo, una señal para actuar, y no solo un proceso diplomático por seguir desde la barrera, serán quienes definan las nuevas reglas de la competitividad regional. Relacionado Maria Saucedo María es una periodista experimentada que combina su formación en letras con una visión estratégica de la logística, creando contenido inspirador e informativo para nuestro blog. title: Auto dealers: Is your reinsurance “B” account working for you?
summary: Auto dealers participate in reinsurance programs to generate additional profit streams beyond their sales and service operations.
body_text: Auto dealers participate in reinsurance programs to generate additional profit streams beyond their primary sales and service operations. When customers purchase extended service contracts or other aftermarket products, the premiums paid by customers are pooled together in a reinsurance account. Over time, as claims are paid out, and the extended service and warranty contracts mature, any remaining funds in the reinsurance account, over the reserve requirements can be distributed to the dealer as profit. This can significantly increase the overall profitability of the dealership. Reinsurance programs can provide tax advantages to auto dealers. The premiums collected from customers are often considered tax-deferred income, as they are not taxed until claims are paid out or profits are distributed. This can allow dealers to defer taxes on their reinsurance income, potentially reducing their current tax liability and providing a more favorable cash flow. Investment opportunities Reinsurance programs typically involve investing the pooled premiums in various investment vehicles to generate returns. Dealers can benefit from the investment opportunities within the reinsurance program, especially in the unrestricted “B” account. Unlike the restricted “A” account, the “B” account allows dealers to invest in a wider range of asset classes, including equities and higher-yielding investments, which can potentially provide higher returns over time. For example, in a typical reinsurance program, the “A” account is subject to certain restrictions, such as a maximum allocation of 10% to equities, with the remaining 90% invested in fixed income. Once funds are moved to the “B” account those restrictions no longer apply. One key aspect that dealers should consider when selecting a trustee is the availability of an open-architecture model for “B” account investing. That gives the dealer access to a wide range of investment options beyond those offered by the trustee’s own organization. This flexibility allows dealers to tailor their investment strategy based on their specific financial goals and risk tolerance, potentially leading to better investment performance. Investing “B” account funds Keeping “B” account held in the reinsurance company’s name—typically still held by the trustee—can benefit the dealer by deferring taxable earnings. The “B” account provides dealers with the flexibility to invest in various asset classes, including equities and other higher-yielding investments. However, not all trustees offer total flexibility in terms of investment options. This is where an open-architecture model can provide significant benefits to auto dealers. With an open-architecture model, the trustee does not limit dealers to a predefined list of investments or products offered solely by their organization. Instead, dealers have the freedom to select investments from a broad universe of options, including those outside of the trustee’s organization. The benefits of a thoughtful investment program can be substantial, with the potential for “B” account funds to compound over time on a tax-deferred basis. Too often funds just sit in cash Setting up a reinsurance program can be intensive for dealer representatives, involving attorneys, CPAs, and other professionals. Once the program is in place, dealers can benefit most by staying proactive in managing their funds, given the demands of running their businesses. The result may be that even when funds are earned, dealers leave the money in the “A” account … or simply sitting in cash in the “B” account. A better alternative may be to automatically move funds from “A” to “B” and implementing an automatic investment program. This is where agents and trustees can play a pivotal role as trusted advisors. Agents can work closely with trustees to bridge the gap between the reinsurance company and the dealers, helping dealers fully understand the benefits of their program and how to make the most of it. Trustees, in turn, can provide valuable support as dealers seek to maximize long-term value of “B” account funds. Whether your needs are traditional or highly complex, the UMB corporate trust and agency teams can smooth processing and administration. We’re with you every step of the way. title: 超越自拍：Roblox 的年齡驗證系統如何協助維持年齡核查的即時性
summary: 一套以安全為優先考量、模組化且多模態的行為機器學習系統
body_text: 分享 工程 安全與文明 超越自拍：Roblox 的年齡驗證系統如何協助維持年齡核查的即時性 一套以安全為優先考量、模組化且多模態的行為機器學習系統 發佈者 王希希 發佈日期 2026年8月4日 Roblox 的 臉部年齡估算 系統已處理 3.38 億筆年齡驗證紀錄，協助 Roblox 用戶在平台上解鎖適合其年齡的聊天功能，並存取適合其年齡的遊戲。初步的年齡驗證固然必要，但年齡驗證並不會因自拍照而結束。帳號可能被共享，或轉交給年幼的兄弟姊妹。 惡意行為者可能會試圖探測我們的防禦機制。為了將年齡驗證提升至超越「特定時間點」訊號的層級，我們建置了一個高吞吐量的機器學習層，用以評估帳戶的持續行為是否仍與其隨時間推移的估計年齡相符。我們在特徵層級的模組化設計，能實現高效的模型更新，並快速適應不斷變化的行為模式。 可靠地運作我們的端到端年齡驗證工作流程，既是分散式系統的挑戰，也是機器學習的挑戰。 年齡估算本身就是一個艱鉅的機器學習問題，因為年齡界線並非行為上的斷崖。父母可能與子女享受相同的體驗，且語言會因文化、情境、社群以及年齡而異。沒有任何單一的行為訊號能夠可靠地捕捉那些隨時間推移及在對抗性壓力下而變化的細微行為模式。即使是我們最可靠的真實標籤，也來自於特定選取的人群，因此可能帶有偏見。 在 Roblox 這樣的規模下運作，更增添了複雜性。在每日的推論週期中，我們彙整來自整個平台的行為訊號，在最適合各工作負載的運算堆疊上執行子模型，並將其輸出結果整合為一個經過校準的估計值。 我們的模型範圍從傳統的機器學習分類器，到擁有超過 3 億個參數的多語言變壓器模型。該系統每天處理近 20 億筆帳戶層級的記錄，而訓練過程則運用了近 3,000 萬個高可信度的年齡標籤。 透過內部自主建構整個系統，我們得以獲得所需的透明度與控制權，以審查所有特徵與訊號是否符合隱私要求，這正是核心的設計要件。 我們還能運用 Roblox 專屬的訊號，捕捉帳號隨時間推移的使用模式——這類縱向脈絡是獨立的外部估算器無法單憑自身擁有的。這也讓我們能掌控完整的機器學習生命週期。我們可以隨著各種模態的可用性進行整合，並針對 Roblox 安全工作流程校準輸出結果，同時在行為變化時監控、控制及更新個別組件。 選擇合適的訊號來預測年齡 不同年齡層的用戶在遊戲、溝通及平台互動模式上，使用 Roblox 的方式各不相同。為了捕捉行為的多樣性，我們將輸入資料細分為不同的訊號類別： 社交情境： 彙整使用者社交圈中的模式，包括其連結對象及互動頻率。 體驗參與度： 超越單純遊戲內容的彙總模式，涵蓋玩家何時遊玩、停留時間長短，以及參與度隨時間的變化趨勢。 帳號與平台活動： 彙總平台使用情況與生命週期訊號，例如帳號使用年限、活動頻率，以及會話層級的行為。 溝通模式： 透過模型推導出的年齡相關語言使用摘要，包含溝通模式在不同情境與時間軸上的變化。 學習得出的使用者表徵： 能捕捉更廣泛使用模式的高階表徵。我們與「探索與個人化」機器學習團隊緊密合作；那些用於預測使用者接下來可能與哪些內容互動的豐富表徵，經過後訓練後，也能用於預測廣泛的年齡區間。 每個訊號類別皆配有符合其資料特性的模型。稀疏、高維度的聚合訊號由梯度提升決策樹（例如 XGBoost 分類器）處理；文本則由微調後的多語言變換器編碼器（mmBERT）處理；而使用者表徵則饋入某些緊湊的神經網路（多層感知器）。 每個子模型預測的目標相同：一組年齡區間的機率分佈。隨後，梯度提升式元學習器會將這些機率向量整合為最終的校準估計值。 基於模組化、運算速度及可解釋性等考量，我們刻意選擇了這種決策層融合方法，而非單一的特徵層模型。系統的模組化設計使我們能夠在不重建整個系統的情況下，新增、重新訓練或停用子模型。這也讓我們能夠更迅速地因應因自然演變或對抗性壓力所導致的行為模式變化。 融合層會讀取每個子模型最新提升的輸出結果，以便運用最佳可用訊號，並在某個訊號缺失或延遲時平穩降級。由於每種模態皆以獨立輸入的形式進入，我們能追蹤哪些訊號群組正驅動決策變化，並在輸出結果被下游系統使用前進行校準與品質把關。 我們在融合層強制執行校準，因為在安全系統中，可預測性比純粹的準確性更為重要。我們對模型進行校準，使其提供值得信賴的信心分數。如此一來，若下游行動將對使用者造成重大影響，我們便能在採取後續行動前，要求更強的證據及更高的信心分數。 標籤中的選擇偏誤 我們信心度最高的標籤來自已完成嚴格年齡驗證的用戶。這些標籤雖具參考價值，但並非 Roblox 用戶的隨機樣本。對於可能影響用戶存取權限的系統而言，代表性是訓練目標的核心部分。 標記樣本群體並非目標群體。完成更嚴格年齡驗證的用戶，在系統層面上與更廣泛的用戶群體存在差異。若以該群體為基礎訓練模型，模型不僅會學習年齡資訊，更可能過度學習「哪些人選擇完成驗證流程」的特徵。為降低此選擇偏誤，我們會重新權重訓練與評估資料，使標記樣本更能反映我們欲進行評分的目標群體。 我們與用戶研究團隊進行跨職能合作，利用彙總的調查結果來制定用於加權的目標人口定義。在此基礎上，我們運用逆傾向加權和迭代比例擬合（即「raking」）等技術，同時在多個維度上調整加權樣本，而非僅針對單一因素進行獨立校正。 並非每個高可信度的來源都能產生可用的訓練範例。標籤的可靠性取決於其背後的驗證事件。某些事件可能包含使模型訓練效果不佳的訊號，例如異常的驗證模式或帳戶完整性疑慮。 我們致力於在訓練前透過「完整性感知標籤過濾」或「 自信學習（Confident Learning） 」等標籤錯誤識別方法來清理標籤，以移除那些在行為建模中看似「分布外」的範例。早期實驗顯示，此類清理有助於防止模型過擬合，並能帶來穩定的效能提升。 在 Roblox 規模下的訓練、推論與避免偏差 推論需要足夠頻繁地執行以保持訊號的新鮮度，但各訊號類別的訓練頻率可能有所不同。我們根據特徵漂移、模型穩定性及模型成本來選擇重新訓練時程。變化迅速或品質快速下降的訊號可以更頻繁地重新訓練；而模型較重且性能變化較緩慢的訊號，則可以較少頻率地重新訓練，或視需求而定。 運算堆疊會配合工作負載的特性進行調整。我們使用 Apache Spark 進行大規模結構化轉換，採用 Ray 框架 處理 GPU 支援的工作負載，並運用生產環境工作程序進行即時訊號處理。 以 Roblox 的規模而言，每天重建每個帳戶的完整歷史紀錄也並不切實際。 我們的自建資料處理框架針對高流量訊號維持有限範圍的滾動歷史紀錄，並分階段執行耗資源的轉換。這使我們每天能處理並彙總數百萬筆帳號層級的記錄，同時獨立擴展大規模的資料擴展、聯結及特徵彙總。這種混合式生產設計讓我們能直接與資料倉儲整合、在模型元件間實現可重現的執行，並在關鍵處存取加速運算資源。 為在現有規模下維持系統穩定性，我們在特徵管道中貫徹兩項嚴格的設計決策： 儲存衍生特徵： 我們盡可能儲存衍生特徵，而非原始活動串流。我們僅保留建模所需的訊號，而非其背後的完整歷史紀錄。 統一的資料合約： 訓練與推論皆採用相同的資料合約。此舉可減少機器學習系統中最常見的失敗模式之一：訓練資料與實際服務資料之間的偏差。 我們在生產生命週期的兩個環節採用閘門機制。首先，模型推廣與模型訓練是分開進行的。候選模型必須通過安全防護檢查，才有資格投入生產推論。若候選模型未能通過安全防護檢查，管道將阻斷推廣流程，並持續提供最新已推廣的合格版本。 其次，推論輸出在傳送至下游之前會經過閘控。自動化檢查機制會偵測品質退化及預測分佈的顯著偏移。若檢查失敗，發布步驟將被阻擋。在與面向用戶的安全工作流程相關聯的機器學習系統中，「今日暫不採取行動」往往比發布無法解釋的分佈偏移更為安全。 系統評估 對於此類系統而言，單一的準確度數值並無太大意義。我們會從排序品質、校準度、長期穩定性，以及重要年齡區間邊界附近的行为表現等面向，來評估模型品質。我們亦將評估資料的代表性視為衡量問題的一部分，因為只有當整體改善能反映系統所服務的目標群體時，該改善才具有實質意義。 在這個加權且保留的評估資料上，融合模型達到了超過 0.9 的平均精確度。其高可信度估計值在每日之間也保持一致，超過 99% 的案例在連續數天內仍維持在同一個大致的年齡區間內。 我們還將該模型與透過「信任與安全」工作流程，由受過訓練的人工審核員產出的獨立真實標籤進行比較。在高信心水準下，該模型對成年人的年齡區間估計，有超過 80% 的時間與人工共識標籤一致。 離線評估僅是其中一環。在實際運作中，使用者行為會因季節性變化、產品上市以及對抗性攻擊而產生變化。正因如此，在將輸出結果應用於下游流程之前，我們會將模型評估指標與對預測分佈、漂移及穩定性的持續監測相結合。我們同時也會監控後續年齡核查的結果，藉此透過實際運作回饋來評估模型的可靠性，並指出應調整閾值或審查路徑之處。 下一步 透過內部自主開發此系統，我們得以安全地運用 Roblox 專屬的訊號、以極其嚴謹的態度運作，並持續進行迭代。 展望未來，我們將專注於優化子模型、推論及衡量機制。在持續推進各層級發展的同時，我們亦將秉持模組化、校準、隱私保護及生產環境防護措施等運作原則。
